description: We are two Applied Mathematics students at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, interested in data science, programming, and space exploration. For the Martian Map challenge, we aim to develop an interactive map using NASA data to visualize the Martian surface, explore different locations, and help future astronauts plan safe routes. We want to combine our analytical skills, technical knowledge, and creativity to build a practical and user-friendly solution.
summary:
Exploring Mars is not just about reaching a destination. It's also about unserstanding the landscape, knowing what makes a location scientifically interesting, and finding a reasonable way to get there. 
That's the idea behind Marswalk Mission Planner, a web application created by our team, Ares Atlas.
We focused on Athabasca Valles, a region of Mars with fascinating geological features. Using data from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Mars Odyssey missions, we built an interactive map that bring together terrain imagery, elevation and slope information, and scientific context.
Users can explore the area, choose one of four potential research locations, and see an experimental route plotted across the Martian surface.The application also explains how each route is calculated and what terrain-related challenges still need further investigation.
Our goal was to make complex NASA data easier to explore and connect it to practical questions about future Mars missions. We believe that understanding the terrain is an important first step toward planning meaningful scientific exploration.
details:
We wanted to see what planning a research trip on Mars could look like if we brought different kinds of NASA data into one place. Instead of trying to map the entire planet, we focused on a small area in Athabasca Valles.

We created Marswalk Mission Planner, a website where you can explore real Martian terrain, choose between four possible research locations, and see a route from a starting point. You can also check the distance, terrain slopes, and other information that helps explain why a particular route was chosen.

For the map and terrain analysis, we worked with HiRISE data from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. We also used geological information based on THEMIS observations from Mars Odyssey to better understand the region.

We built the application with React, TypeScript, and OpenLayers. For route planning, we used Dijkstra's algorithm and a cost model that takes terrain-related factors into account. We worked on different parts of the project, combined them into one application, and tested the result. Our final version passed 171 automated tests.

We know our routes aren't ready for real astronauts. Some terrain features still need closer examination, and our research locations are preliminary. But that's also part of what we wanted to show: planning a route on Mars isn't just about finding the shortest way between two points.

Our project is a small example of how NASA data can be used to explore those decisions in a more practical and understandable way.

Website: https://ares-atlas-marswalk.vercel.app/
